q: Two teams disagree about why the first useful alert sat unread. What should the review establish before assigning a corrective action?
options: Who opened the ticket and when, which queue received it, and how that queue was staffed
Whose name appeared on the published shift roster and whether their previous reviews noted delays
Whether the alert's technical details were identical to those in other incidents that month
Whether an executive has already accepted the final incident summary and severity rating
explanation: A sourced timeline and the actual queue conditions expose the delay mechanism.

q: What makes a post-incident review blameless and still accountable?
options: It assigns equal responsibility to every participating team and rotates future incident leads
It examines the conditions behind decisions and assigns concrete improvements to owners
It publishes participant names and asks each individual to document a personal improvement
It omits disputed decisions and shares only the undisputed recovery steps with leadership
explanation: The review studies decisions in context and creates accountability for future corrective work.

q: The case record says 08:25Z was when the SOC noticed the incident. The first observed malicious event was 06:12Z. What belongs in the review?
options: 131 minutes from the earliest rule match to the time captured in the case record
125 minutes bounded by the first and last recorded malicious activity in the dataset
133 minutes from the first observed malicious event to the recorded notice time
Six hours from the time the SOC noticed the activity to the reporting deadline
explanation: Dwell time uses the first observed malicious event and the notice time.

q: An investigator finds an earlier event consistent with the incident, but cannot yet link it to the case. How should the timeline change?
options: Replace the start time and label the revised duration as the only reliable measure in the report
Remove the candidate from the review and discard the supporting record until a later incident confirms it
Change the notice time by the same amount to keep comparisons with the prior dashboard stable
Record it as a candidate with its source and preserve the current dwell calculation pending corroboration
explanation: Separate uncertain evidence from the confirmed incident window until corroboration is available.

q: Which entry gives a later reader the clearest basis to reproduce a timeline finding?
options: A UTC timestamp, a source record identifier, and a clear observation label
A local timestamp, a manager's recollection, and the severity of the incident
The current ticket status, a dashboard image, and the review facilitator's initials
The alert subject line, the workstation owner's name, and the title of the shift report
explanation: A common time base and a specific source make the observation reproducible.

q: A process event is recorded at 06:14Z. A reviewer says it was triggered by the document downloaded at 06:12Z. How should these statements be recorded?
options: Record the process event and document link as confirmed because the timestamps are close together
Record the process event as observed and label the claimed link to the document as inferred
Record the document link as observed and treat the logged process start as an unverified inference
Combine the statements into a single confirmed event so the report contains fewer timeline rows
explanation: Temporal order supports a hypothesis, while a causal link requires independent evidence.

q: Which owner assignment gives an action item the clearest accountability?
options: List every team that receives the queue and let the teams choose their own completion dates
Assign the action to the incident channel and close it when nobody raises a further concern
Assign one accountable queue owner, a due date, and a replay-based acceptance check
Split accountability equally among all responders and use the next tabletop as a provisional deadline
explanation: An individual owner, a deadline, and a test make closure independently verifiable.

q: A remediation ticket says the alert route was changed. What evidence best supports closing the corresponding review action?
options: The routing administrator marks the configuration ticket as implemented and forwards a screenshot
The next shift report shows a shorter queue, without identifying which alerts reached the duty analyst
The old route is present in the change log and the new route has a descriptive name
A controlled replay produces a ticket in the right queue and the duty analyst acknowledges it on time
explanation: A replay through the actual workflow verifies delivery and acknowledgment at the intended boundary.

q: The team knows the incident notice time and recovery time but never recorded when isolation took effect. How should time to contain be shown?
options: Unavailable, with the missing effective-isolation timestamp and the evidence needed to recover it
Equal to time to recover, because recovery necessarily includes all effective containment actions
Equal to time to acknowledge, because acknowledgment indicates ownership of the entire containment plan
Zero minutes, with a note that containment was complete before the next scheduled status update
explanation: A metric needs evidence for both endpoints and recovery does not establish when isolation took effect.

q: Which wording most directly turns individual blame into a system finding?
options: The primary reviewer should pay more attention to high-priority alerts during future shifts
The overnight queue had no assigned backup when its primary reviewer was unavailable
The overnight analyst was careless and needs extra supervision whenever case volume rises
The shift manager should remind responders that missing an urgent alert is unacceptable
explanation: The backup coverage finding identifies a condition the organization can fix and verify.

q: A dashboard tracks the delay from a rule match at 06:14Z to notice at 08:25Z. What is the proper interpretation?
options: 133 minutes of dwell, since any matching event establishes the beginning of observed activity
125 minutes of active span, since the acknowledgment timestamp closes the measurement window
131 minutes of match-to-notice delay, a different measure from the full dwell interval
Six minutes to acknowledge, because the incident lead took ownership at 08:31Z
explanation: The rule match is two minutes after the first observed malicious event.

q: A report combines detection telemetry and the incident ticket into one timeline. What preserves the distinction between the two lanes?
options: Normalize all times to UTC and group the entire sequence under the incident declaration
Deduplicate records by minute and keep the row that carries the highest severity in that minute
Use the ticket history as the main timeline and put the telemetry rows in an unsorted attachment
Label malicious activity and defender decisions separately while retaining a common UTC axis
explanation: Separate lanes show what happened and when the team learned or acted.

q: Which document should the facilitator bring to a post-incident review?
options: A provisional sourced timeline, the incident decision record, and a list of uncertainties
A polished causal account, preassigned actions, and a slide ranking responders by performance
A generic incident template, a blank attendance register, and the org chart for the SOC
A recovery dashboard, a list of host owners, and the executive presentation from the prior incident
explanation: The facilitator brings evidence and unresolved questions for participants to test and extend.

q: A stakeholder claims missing endpoint alerts were the root cause of the initial compromise. What is the best response?
options: Classify the alert absence as the only root cause because it delayed the beginning of containment
Separate the entry mechanism from the missed detection opportunity and identify evidence for each
Describe both mechanisms as established facts so each can be assigned to a responsible team
Remove endpoint alerting from the review because monitoring begins after the initial compromise
explanation: An entry mechanism and a detection gap can both matter while requiring distinct evidence and actions.

q: Which action is both specific and measurable in a post-incident report?
options: The SOC should improve overnight monitoring and send management a progress summary each month
The team should be more proactive when new high-severity alerts arrive outside business hours
By Friday, the queue lead will verify overnight coverage with a scheduled test alert
The operations group should update its documentation when the updated monitoring roadmap is approved
explanation: The proposed owner, date, and test define an observable acceptance condition.

q: The first responder worked from a stale dashboard during the incident. What question best supports a useful review?
options: Why did the responder use the stale dashboard even though analysts later reconstructed the correct sequence?
Which incident responder would have reached the right conclusion if given the same stale information?
Who last approved the dashboard design, and when should their role in the incident be escalated?
What signals showed dashboard freshness at the time, and what alternatives were available to that responder?
explanation: Reconstruct the information available at decision time to identify actionable interface or process gaps.

q: An action has no due date but has a named owner and a detailed proposed fix. What is still missing?
options: A scheduled commitment that lets the review owner track whether the fix is overdue
A second accountable owner from a separate team who can take over the implementation
An additional description of the incident's every event before the action can enter the tracker
A new incident identifier separate from the parent case and the individual implementation ticket
explanation: Without a date the owner and reviewers cannot consistently track delivery.

q: One team quotes a 133-minute dwell time as exact. What qualification matters for the Banyan exercise?
options: The interval begins at the first rule match and ends when the containment team completes recovery
The start is the first malicious event observed in the available data and the notice time comes from the exercise case record
The measured endpoint is the reporting deadline, regardless of whether the notification was actually sent
The interval assumes all missing endpoint records occurred after the first known detection opportunity
explanation: The earliest observed record and the exercise notice timestamp bound what the exercise can measure.

q: Which question belongs in the report's impact section rather than its action register?
options: Who owns the upcoming queue change and when must it be tested?
When will a follow-up replay be scheduled and who will collect the output?
What services, data, and users were affected, and with what confidence?
Which team will verify completion and who approves any deadline extension?
explanation: The impact section records what the incident affected and the confidence in that assessment.

q: Two sources log times in UTC and IST. How should a reviewer avoid ordering their events incorrectly?
options: Convert UTC entries to whatever timezone the ticket browser currently displays and discard the preserved source offset
Sort the rows by their written clock values and use the ticket order to resolve obvious discrepancies
Round each row to the nearest hour and infer order from the severity attached to each event
Convert both to UTC for comparison and retain the original timestamps and offsets in the evidence record
explanation: Canonical timestamps allow valid sorting and original values preserve the evidence trail.

q: What is the most appropriate way to present an unresolved causal claim in the final review?
options: State it as a hypothesis, explain what supports it, and name the missing evidence
Present it as the likely root cause and remove the uncertainty from the executive version
Keep it out of the review entirely until all responders agree on how the incident started
Put it in the action register as a verified issue and reopen the timeline if it proves incorrect
explanation: An explicit hypothesis preserves the reasoning without overstating what the available records establish.

q: A ticket was opened at 08:25Z and its incident lead acknowledged it at 08:31Z. What interval can these records establish?
options: Six minutes from first rule match to acknowledgment, because both records describe the same alert
Six minutes from notice to acknowledgment, if the case identifies ticket creation as notice
Six minutes from first malicious activity to declaration, because the ticket opens the incident clock
Six minutes to contain, provided the lead was authorized to approve endpoint isolation at acknowledgment
explanation: The record supports the interval between notice and acknowledgment given those event definitions.

q: A review committee wants to close an action because the change shipped. What should it check first?
options: Whether the team shipped other changes in the same deployment that affected ticket categories
Whether the incident was assigned a new severity by the operational manager after recovery
Whether the agreed verification shows the intended change works in the relevant workflow
Whether the action owner gave the same completion date in both the technical and executive summaries
explanation: Implementation alone does not demonstrate that the intended control works.

q: An executive asks whether faster notice would have prevented the whole incident. What can the review responsibly conclude?
options: Earlier notice would necessarily have prevented the initial event because the responder could have contained it immediately
Earlier notice would always have prevented every later event once a matching rule had appeared in the dataset
Earlier notice cannot have helped because the observed active span and dwell time are different intervals
Earlier notice may have enabled earlier response, but any prevented impact is a counterfactual requiring stated assumptions
explanation: A timeline shows opportunities, while a hypothetical outcome depends on response timing and effectiveness.

q: What makes a review report useful to the next shift after the immediate incident has ended?
options: A concise timeline, residual risks, and owned actions with clear verification criteria
A complete copy of all raw records, open chat threads, and shift rosters in chronological order
A one-line root cause, an incident severity number, and links to previous executive reports
A list of approved containment decisions, with no indication of remaining risks or follow-up tasks
explanation: The next shift needs a usable record of what happened and what still requires attention.
